A1.justification: Both PDFs describe StableMTL. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original seven-task experiments, architectural and training ablations, qualitative predictions, and additional appendix metrics.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds NYUv2 comparisons, in-domain evaluation, further ablations, and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The two-stage UNet architecture, task tokens, latent MSE, gradient isolation, task attention, and masking remain unchanged. However, v2 Appendix I describes parallel batch inference, whereas v1 and v2's limitations describe sequential prediction. This inconsistency prevents establishing whether the inference procedure actually changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds NYUv2 training and evaluation on real indoor data under partial supervision (Table 3). This extends coverage from v1's synthetic-only training and real-world generalization setting to learning within a real dataset. The original seven tasks and original datasets remain.

E2.justification: MTPSL, previously discussed but not evaluated, becomes a reported comparator alongside JTR and DiffusionMTL in v2's NYUv2 comparison. The original main comparison retains its comparator membership; identifying the single-task baseline as Lotus-D adds documentation rather than establishing a replacement.

E3.justification: v2 introduces NYUv2's One and Random annotation regimes, in-domain test-split evaluation, three-task loss-weight and N-to-N controls, and H100 resource benchmarks using 256×256 inputs and seven tasks. The retained main evaluation metrics and image resolutions are unchanged. Removed split specifications do not establish that the original experiments changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds loss-objective and loss-weight ablations, performance-versus-training-step curves, auxiliary-task masking interventions, an N-to-N attention comparison, and computational scaling analyses (Figures 5–8 and Appendices I–K). It removes v1's additional layerwise and shared-projection attention visualizations, while retaining the corresponding quantitative architectural ablation.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures for benchmark performance. v2's additional experiments continue point-estimate reporting without introducing an uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Matched main and appendix numerical tables retain their values. Substantial new results include NYUv2 One-regime semantic mIoU of 47.81 for StableMTL versus 44.47 for DiffusionMTL (Table 3), in-domain aggregate Δm of +1.56 (Table 10), loss-combination results reaching +6.94 (Figure 5b), and resource measurements. These are additional settings and analyses, not improvements to the unchanged main benchmark scores.

T1.justification: The latent-loss, attention, masking, and task-encoding mathematics remain substantively equivalent. Splitting the attention projections across equations in v2 changes notation and presentation. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new empirical loss comparisons do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central contributions, seven-task/eight-benchmark superiority claim, and +83.54 Δm comparison remain. v2 additionally asserts that it is the first to use a generative prior for MTL (Section 2), strengthening the novelty claim beyond v1's description of holistic LDM-based MTL as largely unexplored.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of latent-loss normalization, loss accuracy–memory tradeoffs, sample efficiency, and causal task transfer from masking interventions. It newly cautions that affine-invariant metrics may not reflect downstream performance and softens the semantic-generalization restriction in figure captions. Conversely, v1's deeper-layer attention interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendices A.2–A.4's CLIP token construction, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, accumulation count, training-step counts, and exact evaluation splits/sample counts. It adds baseline-protocol clarification and inference-cost details. Reported stage training times change from 8/12 hours to 10/20 hours, without establishing changed training budgets. Task encodings, resolutions, and the code link remain.

R1.justification: v2 replaces much of the broad architecture survey with targeted positioning against DeMT, InvPT++, BridgeNet, and task-switching approaches. It acknowledges existing reductions of quadratic task interactions and distinguishes StableMTL through its generative prior, limited architectural modifications, two-stage training, and partial annotations. This substantively revises the novelty argument rather than merely updating references.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and task-conditioning/loss explanations are substantially rewritten. Main results are divided into domain-generalization and single-dataset evaluations, the latent loss receives a separate explanation, and the appendices are reorganized into sections A–K with references moved after them.

P2.justification: v2 changes from single-column to two-column layout, shortens and moves the introductory montage onto the first page, adds several tables and analytical panels, and combines retained plots with new analyses. It removes the standalone single-stream diagram and supplementary attention plots, while substantially resizing and relocating retained figures and tables.

improvement.justification: The new NYUv2 comparisons, loss and task-transfer ablations, and scalability measurements strengthen evidence missing from v1. However, v2 removes essential reproducibility details and introduces unresolved inconsistencies: sequential versus parallel inference, milliseconds in Table 12 versus seconds in its discussion, and Figure 7's best-performance claim despite the text reporting +3.92 versus +4.07. These substantive gains and losses prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
